authoredPrompt: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for rotating the upper carbon from 0 to 90 degrees; the p orbitals move from parallel overlap to perpendicular separation while an overlap or pi-bond-strength indicator falls, making pi-bond breaking the cost of rotation.
- Toggle between aligned p orbitals and broken pi bond after rotation; the same carbon framework remains in place while the orbital faces switch orientation, clarifying that sideways overlap exists only when the p orbitals are parallel.
authoredContext:
Although essentially free rotation around single bonds is possible (another section), the same is not true of double bonds. For rotation to occur around a double bond, the π bond must break and re-form (the figure). Thus, the barrier to double-bond rotation must be at least as great as the strength of the π bond itself, an estimated 350 kJ/mol (84 kcal/mol). Recall that the barrier to bond rotation in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol.

The π bond must break for rotation to take place around a carbon–carbon double bond.

An orbital diagram with two parallel p orbitals before rotation. After rotation the p orbitals are perpendicular, which breaks the double bond.

The lack of rotation around carbon–carbon double bonds is of more than just theoretical interest; it also has chemical consequences. Imagine the situation for a disubstituted alkene such as 2-butene. (Disubstituted means that two substituents other than hydrogen are bonded to the double-bond carbons.) The two methyl groups in 2-butene can either be on the same side of the double bond or on opposite sides, a situation similar to that in disubstituted cycloalkanes (another section).

discrepancies: In the rotated 90° state the source shows the upper carbon's entire framework (sigma stubs and dashed reference line) rotated with its p orbital; the generated figure rotates only the orbital and leaves the stubs/dashed line fixed, so the broken-bond state doesn't match the source's right panel

Lobe orientation differs: in the source both p orbitals point straight up/down with the carbons offset diagonally, while the generated figure puts the C–C axis vertical on screen and the lobes splayed left/right along the depth axis
Lobes are closed teardrops pointed at both ends and read as round blobs; the source lobes have rounded tips with a pronounced pinch at the nucleus (classic p-orbital shape)
The source's parallel guides form a full parallelogram enclosing the overlap region; the generated figure shows only two thin vertical connector lines
Dashed reference lines appear at both carbons, but in the source the dashed line appears only at the upper/rotated carbon
evaluation.notes: A faithful, pedagogically strong single-scene version of the two-panel π-bond figure: colors, pink/blue lobes, dots, guides, and captions all read correctly, and the twist slider with cos(θ) overlap readout is exactly the right interaction; main weaknesses are the blobby lobe shape, the non-rotating upper framework in the 90° state, and the up/down vs depth-axis orientation difference.
